title: Dantzig-Wolfe Decomposition for Integer Linear Programming
contribution: Textbook chapter extending Dantzig-Wolfe to integer programs (convexification, discretization), proving when the master bound beats the LP bound, with block structures, reverse DW, structure detection and ten examples.
problem_entry: Almost all Dantzig-Wolfe applications are integer programs; the chapter makes integrality inside the pricing domain D the lever and asks, at the root node, what bound and structure a grouping of constraints into A and D buys; for detection, a solver sees only the flat LP/MPS model (pp. 4-5, 60).
key_idea: Represent the integer pricing set D by conv(D) (Minkowski-Weyl) or by a finite integer set T including interior points (Hilbert-Giles-Pulleyblank); both give the same RMP and the bound z_LP <= z_MP <= z_ILP and differ only in where one branches and cuts (x or lambda); no bound gain if the pricing formulation has the integrality property (pp. 6-7, 11-14, 20, 24, 27).
assumptions: Pure ILP, x in Z^n_+, feasible and finite (MILP by remark only); rational data and shortest integer-scaled rays for discretization; linear encoding functions except for a finite D; single-bordered block-diagonal, identical, binary and semi-assignment structures; MIPLIB matrices (ns1778858, b2c1s1, 10teams, ic97_potential) only as pictures (pp. 5, 11-13, 21-22, 29, 40-41, 60-63).
proof_devices: bound ordering z_LP <= z_MP <= z_IMP = z_ILP by a chain of feasible-domain inclusions (4.8) (p. 7)
existence of the finite discretization set T by splitting each ray multiplier into fractional and integer parts (4.15)-(4.17) (pp. 11-12)
x-integrality redundant under discretization: integer points times binary or integer multipliers stay integer (Prop 4.3, pp. 14-15)
interior integer points dominated by extreme points, so pricing never generates them at the root (structural deficiency, Note 4.8, p. 20)
integrality property of the pricing formulation makes the master and LP feasible regions equal (Props 4.7 and 4.13, pp. 27, 39)
disaggregation of identical blocks as a zero-cost balanced transportation problem filled greedily (Prop 4.10, p. 36)
non-linear costs exact under discretization of a finite D: a binary lambda picks one point and B&B bounds stay monotone (Prop 4.14, p. 41)
numerical counterexample for unbounded domains: quadratic cost at (9,4) gives 97 versus 73 (p. 42)
necessity in Prop 4.17 by contradiction: scale a fractional point by an integer x0 into an integer ray the given points cannot express (p. 58)
reverse Dantzig-Wolfe by exhibiting a compact formulation whose reformulation yields the given column model (Props 4.15-4.17, pp. 53-58)
Lagrangian bound z_RMP + sum_k c^k <= z_MP <= z_RMP, valid for arbitrary duals (Prop 4.12 and (4.68), pp. 38-39)
experiments: No benchmark campaign (no test set, hardware, seeds or time limits): ten toy examples, e.g. nine TCSPP pricing domains with bounds 7 to 13 against z_ILP = 13 (Table 4.6, p. 80), z_LP from 3.900 to 3.020 as big-M grows from 25 to 1000 (Tables 4.8-4.9, pp. 84, 86), one scene-selection instance with CPLEX 11.2 (IP gap 58.8% compact versus 1.1% master, Table 4.10, p. 97); negative results reported (pp. 81-82, 87, 91, 95, 106, 110).
positioning: Builds on Minkowski-Weyl, Hilbert/Giles-Pulleyblank via Nemhauser-Wolsey, Vanderbeck-Wolsey and Geoffrion, with Lagrangian relaxation as the dual view; plays devil's advocate with Held-Karp and Ford-Fulkerson; credits a PhD student (Prop 4.5) and Villeneuve (Prop 4.15), flags new results, and credits Bergner et al. 2015 and GCG for structure detection (pp. 11, 27-28, 111-113).
writing: Joint textbook voice with an epigraph, a running atoms-versus-molecules analogy (Soumis), joke-titled notes, a boxed one-line lesson opening each example, explicit hedging where theory stops, and exercises on history and trick questions (pp. 1, 4, 14, 27, 65, 67-107, 113-114).
limits_future: Root node only (branching in ch. 7); MILP only by remark; non-linear encodings on unbounded domains and the mixed-integer non-linear case left open (error-bound question, Note 4.14 conjecture); bound-pricing trade-off sometimes impossible to predict; decomposition scores are proxies; Exercise 4.21 asks for further useless reformulations (pp. 4, 27, 42-43, 64, 120).

method_links.note: Success is measured against the compact formulation; a reformulation is a detour at zero integrality gap; Prop 4.7 gives the no-bound-gain case; reverse Dantzig-Wolfe keeps a compact model in view for branching and cutting (step 6); branch-and-price presented as general for MILPs while tailoring helps. Also H5 (the formulation, not the problem, carries the integrality property, p. 67; compact formulations are not created equal, p. 110), H1 (partial pricing p. 29, multi-commodity Dijkstra pricing pp. 94-95, a pricing filter must show no false negatives p. 82) and Taste G4 (structured versus unstructured models, p. 65).

The stop rule (no bound gain, stay with branch-and-cut) is narrower than the chapter: Dantzig-Wolfe is called an ideal choice for the multi-commodity flow at z_MP = z_LP because the master has under 0.001% of the compact rows, scene selection and student teams are reformulated for symmetry and a quadratic objective, and graph-based detection may handle unstructured models.

Nine TCSPP pricing domains computed and tabulated (redundant constraints shrink the column set without raising the bound; one inflow-bound family closes the gap); candidate decompositions enumerated (2^l constraint-class subsets, hundreds or thousands) and scored by proxies, the best bound being no goal; no single decomposition; learned structure cited; checkpoint in the authors' words ('don't be deluded by the beauty'); an open conjecture published (Note 4.14).

The only timed comparison is one scene-selection instance with CPLEX 11.2 and no hardware stated, under a general lead sentence ('Exploiting the structure helps a lot!'); the pricing strategy is explicitly left to experiments.

One notation across convexification, discretization and their block variants; open questions published (error bound for non-linear costs, Note 4.14 conjecture, partition refinement not exploited, Exercise 4.21); a PhD student's observation credited as Prop 4.5 and Villeneuve credited for Prop 4.15 (step 6).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Name what the reformulation buys: bound, size, symmetry or non-linear cost
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A bound gain needs a pricing formulation without the integrality property (Prop 4.7), yet the chapter recommends Dantzig-Wolfe for the multi-commodity flow at z_MP = z_LP because the master has 10,000 rows against 999,010,000, for scene selection because day symmetry disappears, and for student teams because a quadratic cost becomes column costs; Held-Karp and Ford-Fulkerson exploit the integrality property.

Semi-assignment rows go to the master because reformulating them returns the compact model (Prop 4.5, generalized assignment); integrality-breaking constraints and the constraints that matter (time bounds) go into pricing; redundant constraints in pricing shrink the column set without raising the bound; identical blocks are aggregated.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Audit a pricing-domain filter for false negatives; a rule never relaxed is a constraint
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Table 4.7 classifies the nine TCSPP paths as N, P, FN or FP against both the master LP and the integer optimum for an arc-count rule; a rule never turned off must show no false negatives with respect to integrality; a practical rule that would reject a better solution anyway is really a constraint of the problem.

transferable: Integrality-property screen before building: if the pricing formulation (shortest path, assignment, circulation) has the integrality property, the master bound equals the LP bound (Props 4.7, 4.13, pp. 27, 39; cases pp. 90, 95).
Bound-ladder table on a toy instance: a sequence of pricing domains built by adding constraint subsets, with master size, z_MP and ceil(z_MP) against z_LP and z_ILP (Table 4.6, p. 80).
False-negative/false-positive table for a heuristic restriction of the pricing domain, judged against the master-LP optimum and the integer optimum (Table 4.7, p. 82).
Big-M sensitivity row: report z_LP for M = 25, 50, 100, 500, 1000 (Tables 4.8-4.9, pp. 84, 86).
Disaggregate an aggregated identical-block solution by greedily filling a zero-cost transportation problem (p. 36) or by the lexicographic formula (4.184) of Exercise 4.9 (p. 115).
Keep the aggregated convexity constraint as sum(lambda_p) - v = 0 with a static variable v in [0, kappa] whose bounds branching changes (p. 50).
Blocks that need not be used: binary x0^k with D^k x^k >= d^k x0^k and x^k <= u^k x0^k, giving <= 1 convexity rows (pp. 46-48).
Reverse Dantzig-Wolfe check for any column model: write the compact formulation it reformulates (Props 4.15-4.17) and confirm it keeps the real decision variables (pp. 53-58, 110).
Structure detection by constraint classes: try subsets of whole classes as the border and count connected components of the remaining bipartite graph (p. 63).
Size argument when there is no bound gain: count rows and columns of the compact model against the master (pp. 93-94).
Initialize column generation for a multi-depot vehicle scheduling problem from the single-depot aggregate solved as a network flow (Exercise 4.20(h), Oukil et al. 2007, p. 120).
coauthors: Jacques Desrosiers, Guy Desaulniers, Jean Bertrand Gauthier (four-author book S017; joint voice, no passage attributable to Lübbecke alone)

quotes.text: Evaluating the success of a reformulation essentially lies in comparing how much it can be solved faster than the compact formulation.
Indeed, the trade-off between the discarded fractional solutions and the difficulty of solving the integer pricing problem appears to be complex and sometimes impossible to predict.
